newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Rao wears trademark pout at court hearing.
newsitem.headline: India's Rao wears trademark pout at court hearing.

text.p: Five months after standing at the pinnacle of Indian politics, former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao sat before a lower court judge on Wednesday at a criminal trial hearing.
Rao arrived at the makeshift court in a convoy of bullet-proof cars that stopped before a battery of television cameras and photographers standing behind a fence.
Expressionless, Rao raised his clasped hands in the traditional Indian greeting and bowed briefly to the press.
Special plainclothes paramilitary commandos whisked him inside the concrete building, surrounded by some 300 local police.

A hush fell over the small, windowless courtroom when Rao entered, ringed by bodyguards and flanked by his lawyer, R.K. Anand. He became the first former or serving prime minister to appear in court on criminal charges.

Wearing his trademark pout, "dhoti" loincloth and beige scarf, Rao sat near the door at the side of the room, his bodyguards standing around him, and apart from three co-accused in the seven-year-old criminal forgery case.
Rao slowly rose to his feet with the others when chief metropolitan magistrate Prem Kumar entered and mounted the temporary bench.
During 3-1/2 hours of arguments, the former prime minister sat impassively, stroking his chin or, his eyes half-closed, clasping his hands before his face.

Lawyers, two dozen reporters and colleagues from Rao's Congress party filled the unadorned white room in a concrete annexe of a spacious conference hall, selected by police as a more secure venue than the teeming local courts.
No television cameras or photographers were allowed inside.

Ghulam Nabi Azad, recently appointed Congress general secretary, and former cabinet ministers Pranab Mukherjee and V.C. Shukla sat in the back of the courtroom in a show of support for the party's former leader.
Rao stepped down as Congress chief in September after a judge upheld a summons ordering him to appear in court in a separate criminal cheating case.
After Kumar adjourned the trial hearing for lunch, Rao left the building surrounded by Azad, Shukla and Mukherjee, and climbed into his car without gesturing to waiting photographers.
It was unknown whether Rao, who had been exempted from attending the hearing but appeared anyway, would return to the court when the proceedings reconvened later in the day.
